title: Explore richer structures
goal: Use multiple index levels, list-valued columns, and categorical encodings.
prerequisites: Understand indexes, reshaping, and basic data types.

cells.title: Create a MultiIndex
cells.explanation: A MultiIndex stores more than one label per row. Here Campus and Student_ID jointly locate a student. sort_index arranges the levels for predictable selection.

questions.answer: A row with Campus RAK and Student_ID S003.

questions.prompt: What Name and Score will appear?
Why keep Student_ID as an additional level?
questions.answer: Campus alone is shared by several students; the second level identifies the individual record.

cells.task: Use xs to select all Dubai students at the Campus level and print Name and Score.
cells.hint: Call xs("Dubai", level="Campus") on the indexed table.
cells.solution:
df = students().set_index(["Campus", "Student_ID"]).sort_index()
result = df.xs("Dubai", level="Campus")[["Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The selection contains six Dubai students; xs drops the selected level by default.

options: Several labels per row or column axis entry
check.feedback: It represents an axis with multiple levels of labels.

cells.solution_verify:
assert len(result) == 6
assert result.index.name == "Student_ID"
assert "S002" in result.index
cells.watch: A tuple used as a MultiIndex key is different from a list of separate row keys.
cells.takeaway: Name index levels so selections are understandable.

cells.title: Stack and unstack
cells.explanation: stack moves column labels into an additional row-index level. unstack moves an index level back into columns. The explicit future_stack=True selects the modern stack implementation on pandas 2.2 and 3.x.

questions.prompt: How many index levels does the stacked result have?
questions.answer: Two: Student_ID and the original measure column label.

questions.prompt: How many values are in the stacked result?
questions.answer: 4, from two students and two measures.

questions.prompt: Were the measurements averaged during stacking?
questions.answer: No. Their labels moved; the original values remain.

cells.task: Stack the first three students and unstack the last level back into a DataFrame. Check that it equals the original wide table.
cells.hint: Use .unstack() on the stacked Series, then .equals(wide).
cells.solution:
wide = students().head(3).set_index("Student_ID")[["Score", "Attendance"]]
stacked = wide.stack(future_stack=True)
result = stacked.unstack().reindex(columns=wide.columns)
print(result)
print("Values restored:", result.equals(wide))
cells.solution_note: The explicit column reindex restores the original column order for the equality check.

check.prompt: Which operation returns the last index level to columns?
check.feedback: unstack reshapes one index level into column labels.

cells.watch: Missing combinations can appear when reshaping sparse data; inspect the resulting shape.
cells.takeaway: Stack and unstack move labels between axes.

cells.title: Expand lists with explode
cells.explanation: Sometimes one cell contains several items, such as a list of skills. explode creates a separate row for each item and repeats the other columns. This changes the unit of analysis from one row per student to one row per student-skill.
cells.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": ["S001", "S002"], "Skills": [["Python", "SQL"], ["Excel"]]})
result = df.explode("Skills", ignore_index=True)
print(result)

questions.prompt: What kind of value is stored in each Skills cell before explode?

questions.answer: 3: two skills for S001 and one skill for S002.

questions.prompt: Why would counting rows after explode overcount students?
questions.answer: A student with multiple skills appears in multiple rows.

cells.task: Give S002 a second skill, SQL. Explode the table, then store the count of student-skill rows for each skill in result as a value_counts() Series.
cells.hint: After explode, use the Skills column value_counts().
cells.solution:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": ["S001", "S002"], "Skills": [["Python", "SQL"], ["Excel", "SQL"]]})
long = df.explode("Skills", ignore_index=True)
result = long["Skills"].value_counts()
print(result)
cells.solution_note: SQL appears twice; Python and Excel appear once each.

check.prompt: After explode, one row represents what?
options: One listed item belonging to a student
check.feedback: Each item becomes a row; the student identifier can repeat.

cells.watch: An empty list becomes a row with a missing item; a string that looks like a list is still a string.
cells.takeaway: Check what a row represents after changing the layout.

cells.title: Order and encode categories
cells.explanation: Categorical values can follow a chosen order instead of alphabetical order. get_dummies makes one indicator column per category. These indicator values describe membership, not a numerical ranking.
cells.code:
df = students().head(4).copy()
df["Program"] = pd.Categorical(df["Program"], categories=["IT", "AI"], ordered=True)
ordered = df.sort_values("Program", kind="stable")
result = pd.get_dummies(ordered["Program"], prefix="Program", dtype=int)
print(ordered[["Student_ID", "Program"]])
print(result)

questions.answer: IT, because it is listed first in the ordered categories.

questions.prompt: What are Program_IT and Program_AI for S001?
Does a dummy value of 1 mean AI is better than IT?
questions.answer: No. It only marks whether that row belongs to the AI category.

cells.task: Change the category order to AI then IT and print the sorted student IDs and dummy columns.
cells.hint: Reverse the categories list before sorting.
cells.solution:
df = students().head(4).copy()
df["Program"] = pd.Categorical(df["Program"], categories=["AI", "IT"], ordered=True)
ordered = df.sort_values("Program", kind="stable")
result = pd.get_dummies(ordered["Program"], prefix="Program", dtype=int)
print(ordered[["Student_ID", "Program"]])
print(result)
cells.solution_note: AI students now appear first; each row still has one indicator value equal to 1.

check.feedback: Each column indicates membership in one category.

cells.watch: Values outside a specified category list become missing; validate allowed categories first.
cells.takeaway: Category order and indicator encoding are separate choices.
